articles.title: Where Lawyers Got The Word ‘Boilerplate’
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Lawyers churn out “boilerplate” every day — the standard, reusable clauses tucked at the end of every contract. But the word has a surprisingly industrial, pre-legal origin, and it didn’t start in a law office at all. Where did “boilerplate” come from?

Hint: It passed through the newspaper business before it ever reached the law, and the very first “boiler plates” were exactly that: made of steel.

See the answer on the next page.

The post Where Lawyers Got The Word ‘Boilerplate’ appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Work-Life Integration For Lawyers Who Want Their Time Back
articles.content:
When I started my coaching business in 2004, I had networking meetings in the morning, more of them at night, and a desk covered in business cards from people I was supposed to follow up with. Most weekends were already spoken for by family commitments. Today, I rarely work nights or weekends, and I can take a morning or an afternoon off without feeling like the whole business will come to a screeching halt. If you’d told me back then that I could have that kind of flexibility, I would’ve asked what the hell you were talking about. Today I’d call it work-life integration.
So, what is work-life integration for lawyers? Where work-life balance can sound like giving work and home equal time every day, work-life integration is about making those commitments fit together over the course of a real week. You might put in a late night before a filing and still be able to take Friday afternoon off. The trouble starts when every night turns into a late night and Friday afternoon is the first thing you give up. The real challenge here is in finding efficiencies that allow you to achieve your goals without adding to your already jam-packed schedule.
Here are three changes that helped me get some control back and that I now work on with lawyers.
Become A Student Of Time Management
When I started my business, I had stacks of paper on my desk, stacks of business cards from people I needed to follow up with and enough unopened emails that finding the one I actually needed felt like a project. At one point, my assistant and I gathered all the loose paperwork into a single pile. It stood four feet high and took us six hours and a label maker to get through. I was glad to have my desk back, but I knew I needed to become a student of time management if I wanted to keep it that way.
That’s where David Allen’s “Getting Things Done” helped me. I started using the Four D’s to decide what to do with every task that landed on my desk, in my inbox or in my head. If it takes less than two minutes, do it. If it requires planning or focused time, defer it and put it on your calendar. If it’s work someone else can handle, and it doesn’t require your level of expertise, delegate it. If it has no business being part of your workday, drop it from the workday. And if it doesn’t need doing at all, take it off the list altogether.
The trick is to use the Four D’s when you’re reviewing what’s come in, not every time your phone buzzes. Otherwise, a two-minute email can pull you away from the brief you finally had time to write. The point isn’t to get better at squeezing things in. It’s to stop giving every task the same claim on your time.
Stop Saying Yes Before You Check What It’ll Cost
There’s something addictive about filling up your calendar. You get invited to a networking event, someone asks you to join a board, and a conference comes up that looks too good to miss. It feels like you’re doing a lot of important things, and some of them are worth doing. But then you look up on Friday and realize you’re behind on billable work, you haven’t followed up with the people you met at last week’s event, and the brief you meant to finish on Thursday is now coming home with you.
Before you say yes, take a look at what’s already on your calendar. If you join that board, look beyond the monthly meeting and ask how much time the work will actually take. If you go to the conference, think about which client work will have to move and whether you’ll have time to follow up with the people you meet. A better question than “Can I fit it in?” is “What am I willing to give up to do this well?” Sometimes the answer will make it easy to say yes. Other times, it’ll give you a good reason to say no.
Here’s what I like to say when the timing isn’t right. “I really appreciate you thinking of me. I have a policy that if I can’t give something 100%, I’d rather not take it on. I can’t give this the time it deserves right now, but I’d be happy to revisit it next year if the timing is better.” Only leave that last door open if you mean it. Most people would rather get a clear, thoughtful no than have to chase you for an answer or count on you for something you don’t have time to do.
Build A Book That Gives You More Say In Your Week
If you’re the person everyone trusts to do the work, it’s easy to spend your whole week doing it. But if you want more say in which clients you serve and how you spend your time, you need to learn how to bring in work of your own. That doesn’t happen by waiting until your billable hours are done and hoping you still have the energy to call someone.
Start with one scheduled hour on your calendar each week and make it non-negotiable. Use it to reconnect with a client, follow up on an introduction, or get to know a referral partner better. As you bring in work, look for pieces of it a capable colleague can handle with your guidance. If you originate every matter and insist on doing every bit of the work yourself, you haven’t bought yourself any flexibility. You’ve just found a way to get busier.
If you’re at a full-service firm, look for cross-marketing opportunities with the clients you already serve. You might spot a need in another practice area, make the introduction and earn origination credit without having to handle the matter yourself. And when you bring in work in your own practice area, think about which matters strong associates or younger partners can handle with your guidance. Learning to bring in work without having to do it all yourself is one of the best ways to gain the freedom and independence you want while becoming more valuable to your firm in a competitive market.
Take a look at next week’s calendar. What’s one thing you could hand off or decline, and what would you do with the time you got back? Make that decision now, while the hour is still yours to give.
Build your book. Own your future. BE THAT LAWYER.
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. articles.title: Can You Legally Ditch Work And Family Chores To Play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ In Peace?
articles.content:
In less than 24 hours, “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be available to play. As one of the most anticipated games ever, there is speculation that its release will negatively affect workplace productivity and divert spending away from other forms of entertainment, including bars and amusement parks.
Rockstar in its infinite wisdom opted to release the game at midnight local time on a work night. Most people will either wait until the next day to play or play the game for a few minutes after midnight before going to bed.
But the true GTA fans will grab their espresso, Red Bull, or their energy drink of choice and play until they crash out at 4 a.m. While some had the foresight to request time off from their job, others did not and will have to choose between going to work half-asleep or not show up to work and explain why to their boss.
Most people will attempt to binge-play the game for hours or even days with no interruptions. To head off family discord, some fans have drafted tongue-in-cheek “leave me alone” contracts. For a set period, the player is exempt from chores and relatives agree to refrain from interruptions or snide remarks.
For employees wanting time off to play the game, planning could help a lot.
Only a few states require giving employees paid time off (PTO) or paid vacation. Employers generally offer PTOs as a fringe benefit. Since PTOs can be used for any reason, including playing a video game, an employee does not have to disclose why he or she is using it. But in most cases, an employee must give their employer adequate notice and the employer must approve the PTO.
If the employer does not have a PTO program, then they can simply request an unpaid time off. But like PTO programs, the employee must get approval from their employer.
Without prior approval, some may be tempted to claim a sick day. Falsely claiming illness can lead to write-ups, poor performance reviews, or termination. True, sleep deprivation and caffeine-fueled mood swings after an all-night session might technically qualify as feeling unwell, but employees who take this route usually prefer not to explain the cause.
If using a sick day is not an option, an employee could tell the boss the truth and hope that mercy will be shown and that the absense will be excused.
Next, let’s consider whether “leave me alone” contracts between family members are enforceable. Before I begin, I strongly advise against using these contracts other than for humor. If you try to enforce the contract, you may end up getting busted by your parents or wasted by your significant other.
First, there must be consideration for the contract to be enforceable. What do the family members get in return for being left alone to play GTA 6? The family members could get money. The player could offer to do double the chores in the future as consideration, but in this case, a firm date to do it should be given or it could be considered too vague to be adequate consideration.
Second, damages for breach would be nearly impossible to calculate. What is the monetary value of interrupted gaming hours? Litigation itself would be impractical. Courts are traditionally reluctant to enforce purely domestic arrangements between family members or cohabiting partners. The law generally presumes that such agreements rest on affection and mutual accommodation rather than an intention to create legal relations. Judges have little interest in policing how much quiet time one partner receives for a video game.
Any serious attempt at a written agreement should at least include an informal dispute-resolution clause pointing the parties toward a family therapist rather than a courtroom.
Most players will enjoy GTA 6 responsibly. For those who don’t, the law offers little help. Without approved time off, save the marathon sessions for the weekend. And while a “leave me alone” contract may earn a laugh (or a groan) from family members, treat it as an informal request for courtesy and not a document you intend to enforce.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email at stevenchungatl@gmail.com. Or you can connect with him on Twitter (@stevenchung) and connect with him on LinkedIn.

articles.title: Deck The Hall With Raises And Bonuses
articles.content:
Choate Hall that is!
Boston firm Choate Hall & Stewart has seen the lights from the Old North Church and sent out a rider to announce “The raises are coming! The raises are coming!” The firm sits right near the top-o-the-second-hundred, boasting a shade over $2 million in revenue per lawyer, and just this year made the jump to expand beyond the flagship office, opening in Manhattan.
But enough background. You want to hear about money, so here we go. The new salaries are:
1st Year — $235,000
2nd Year — $245,000
3rd Year — $270,000
4th Year — $320,000
5th Year — $385,000
6th Year+ — $410,000
Choate pays its “Principals” on a grid as well, with first-years moving up to $440,000 and second-years to $455,000. Patent agents will get $10,000 raises and staff scientists will be bumped up by $7,500.
The memo also joins the special bonus train:
We also want to confirm that in March 2027, in addition to our customary annual market — and, in some cases, above-market — bonuses, we will continue to pay the additional “special” bonus for on-track principals, associates, patent agents and staff scientists who meet their hours requirements for annual bonuses for the 12-month period ending on January 31, 2027, according to the market scale we have used for the past two years:
Patent agents and scientists are getting $6,000. As for the lawyers, they’ll be picking up:
1st Year — $6,000
2nd Year — $10,000
3rd Year — $15,000
4th Year — $20,000
5th Year — $25,000
6th Year+ — $25,000
Principals — $25,000
Folks at the firm for only part of the year — including new first-years — will get prorated special bonuses.
Congratulations, folks.
Remember everyone, we depend on your tips to stay on top of this stuff. So when your firm matches, please text us (646-820-8477) or email us (subject line: “[Firm Name] Matches”). Please include the memo if available. You can take a photo of the memo and send it via text or email if you don’t want to forward the original PDF or Word file.
And if you’d like to sign up for ATL’s Bonus Alerts (which is the alert list we’ll also use for salary announcements), please scroll down and enter your email address in the box below this post. If you previously signed up for the bonus alerts, you don’t need to do anything. You’ll receive an email notification within minutes of each bonus announcement that we publish.
Joe Patrice is a senior editor at Above the Law and co-host of Thinking Like A Lawyer. Feel free to email any tips, questions, or comments. Follow him on Twitter or Bluesky if you’re interested in law, politics, and a healthy dose of college sports news.
